card.identity: Tomas Bell, keeper of the tide archive

changes.value: The tide bell is operated by a manual lever; it cannot ring without someone moving the lever.

commit.text:
The harbour had supplied Lena with three different times for the same tide before she had finished her first cup of tea. The pilot's almanac gave one, the watch board another, and a boy selling folded charts outside the rope shop assured her that both were wrong. She bought the cheapest chart because its paper was dry, then stood beneath the awning until the boy found the change. After paying three coins for the copied chart, Lena had fifteen left. “There are fifteen coins left,” Lena said. It was a small professional expense, but she entered it in the purse book while she could still remember the seller's face. At Merrow Quay, officials had a habit of regarding missing receipts as evidence that the public had never paid. She had come to survey the northern channel, a job that required the town's tide register, and the register had vanished that morning.

Tomas opened the archive with his shoulder because the warped door caught against the first shelf. Inside, the air smelled of salt trapped in paper. He had placed towels beneath two windows and a bowl under a stain in the ceiling, making a household of the town's neglected measurements. Lena admired the arrangement until he asked whether she could complete the survey from a certified copy. She said a copy would be useful after she compared it with the original. He rubbed the pale skin beneath his spectacles. “The bridge is closed,” Tomas said. Through the far window she could see the inspector moving towards it. Rook crossed to the survey bridge and stayed beside its lever. The contradiction did not require an accusation. She asked Tomas what he meant by closed, and he said the public should not use it during the inspection. That was a narrower statement than the one he had first offered.

Lena had borrowed the brass key from the harbour clerk to reach the upper chart room. Tomas said she should not carry it into the rain, where the small ward could fill with grit. She placed the brass key in Tomas’s open hand. He tested the weight before putting it into a drawer that had no lock of its own. Lena knew Tomas now held the brass key. Outside, a figure passed behind the window at the end of the corridor. Ivo still believed Lena had the brass key, although he had watched the handover through the wrong window. The window reflected a mirror on the opposite wall, turning the order of their movements inside out. Lena noticed the watcher only as a dark coat receding towards the quay. Lena no longer trusted Tomas to interpret the archive without a witness. She asked him to leave the drawer open while she worked. He did so, but she could hear his objection in the care with which he moved the chair away from it.

Ivo arrived with a stack of blank forms and an explanation about the watch office needing a delivery signature. The pay register named Ivo Marr as a dock clerk. The clerk had copied that line for Lena earlier, adding a neat tick beside the wages figure. Ivo spoke as if his chief skill was carrying paper from one room to another without asking what it said. Lena gave him the empty forms she did not need and watched him avoid the tide shelf. Ivo carried the missing tide register under his coat. A corner of the leather binding appeared when he reached for his cap. She recognised the green stain the harbour chart had acquired from that same cover. He saw her recognise it and said he had been told to bring it back. She asked by whom. He answered by opening the book instead of naming the person.

The afternoon measurement occupied one page, with the following page already ruled for the next day. The register contained two entries for the same tide. At first Lena assumed the second line was a correction, but there was no crossed figure, explanatory mark, or initial beside either entry. The two observations claimed the same water and different fees. She turned the volume towards the window and examined the stitched edge. A blue thread protruded from the register’s stitched spine. Ivo tried to press it flat with his thumb. She asked him to leave it alone until they knew whether it belonged to the stitching. He said every old register had loose threads. That might be true, and it did not answer why this one lay across an opening in the leather. Tomas set three cups on the desk, making more noise than the crockery required.

Rook came back briefly to ask whether the missing volume had been found. He stood in the doorway rather than approach the open page. Rook wore a square impression of clean skin where his ring should have been. Lena had met him only once before, when he signed the temporary survey permit with a ring tapping the desk at every stroke. Now he folded that hand into his other sleeve. She asked whether the bridge lever was working. He said he would know when the test bell sounded and returned to the rain before she could ask about the second fee. Ivo shut the register. Lena did not stop him, because she had already copied both entries and wanted to know which person would object to her keeping the copy. Nobody did. The silence felt less like agreement than a room full of people waiting for another person to speak first.

They brought the survey marker from the porch before the weather worsened. Tomas fixed the red survey marker to the archive wall. The town used red for a measurement awaiting public verification, a convention Lena liked because it made uncertainty visible instead of disguising it as an incomplete shade of official blue. She reached above the shelf to steady the marker while Tomas drove the pin. The window shutter swung loose behind her. The falling shutter bruised Lena’s right wrist. Pain spread through the joint when she caught the wooden edge. Tomas wanted to send for the nurse at once. She said a bruise could wait until they had secured the shutter, which was still capable of striking someone else. Ivo held the hook while she stepped back. His hands knew the mechanism too readily for someone who claimed never to work in this room.

The rain thickened until the quay vanished behind the glass. Lena could not tell whether the wet footprints belonged to Rook. A person had crossed the corridor while the room was empty, leaving a track that ended at the register shelf. Ivo's boots were wet too. Tomas suggested the marks belonged to the nurse, though no nurse had arrived. Lena drew their outline on a scrap instead of selecting a convenient owner. She had learned that restraint during a winter job in another port, when a familiar boot size had nearly become a public charge. Lena remembered the winter when she had lived above the rope shop. The rope shop smelled warmer than this room, and the landlord had shouted at every customer as though the whole town owed him rent. She could not have named the year without finding an old letter. Remembering it did not tell her who had stood at the tide shelf today.

Tomas explained that the bridge bell gave the watch a signal when the channel was clear. Lena asked him to show the mechanism on the room's engineering plan. There was no automatic trigger, no water-driven chain, and no clock connection: the bell rang when a person moved the lever. He admitted that several official notices had described it as a tide signal without making that distinction. Ivo said everyone understood. Lena asked whether everyone included visitors navigating a narrow channel in fog. If the fog lifted, the northern buoy might become visible. Until then a captain could hear a bell and mistake a person's instruction for a measurement of the sea. Tomorrow, Lena intended to search every boat in the harbour. The search had not happened, and she wrote it under tomorrow rather than describe the boats as cleared. Ivo watched her divide the notebook page with a ruler and seemed, for the first time, interested in what she might discover.

They ate bread beside the copy stand while the rain beat at the shutter. Tomas talked about a hearing proposed for the next morning, as if saying the word public might excuse the room's smaller concealments. Tomas believed a public hearing would be safer than a private bargain. Lena asked him to bring the original register and the watch log. He said he would ask permission. She answered that records kept for the town ought to be available to the town's authorised surveyor. Ivo stared at the bread. He was still holding the register, but now he held it where she could see it. The blue thread had caught on his cuff. She wanted to pull it free, then decided that leaving one small thing undisturbed might be more useful than winning another argument before the evidence had arrived.

Lena remained in the archive when the public doors were locked. Tomas brought a blanket and a lamp whose wick he trimmed too short. The small flame made the copied figures look paler than they were. Lena placed a sheet over them to keep the damp from lifting the ink and listened for the bridge bell. It did not sound. She fell asleep at the copy stand with her wrist resting on the folded blanket. That night she dreamed the tide bell was ringing beneath the sea. In sleep the sound arrived through black water, and the two entries opened like doors beneath it. She woke before dawn to the scratch of someone moving a chair in the corridor. The lamp had gone out. Her purse book, the damp chart, and both copies remained where she had put them. She waited without calling, because the next sound might tell her whether the visitor knew she was awake. Lena settled at the archive desk to wait for morning.

commit.text:
The corridor chair had been moved to hold a note beneath the archive door. It asked Lena to meet the inspector at the bridge before the morning bell, and the signature was a square of ink too blurred to read. She woke Tomas, who said the request was ordinary, then began dressing with an urgency that contradicted the word. They took the long way around the flooded steps. By midnight Lena was standing on the survey bridge. Rain gathered beneath the handrail and fell into the tide in separate silver threads. The bell hung above the lever, still enough to look decorative. Lena checked the linkage before approaching the far rail. It could not have rung during the night without a hand pulling the lever. The note, however, made no claim about whether anyone had heard it ring.

Ivo waited in the shelter beside the bridge office. He had the register in a canvas cover and a folded appointment page under his arm. Tomas asked him to unlock the office if the watch officer came before they returned. Tomas handed the brass key to Ivo before entering the rain. Lena saw the drawer key move between them clearly this time, without mirrors or dark windows to rearrange the gesture. She asked Ivo to say where he would keep it. He put it in his waistcoat and answered, here. Tomas went towards the hall to find the officer who had ordered the inspection. Lena wanted to ask why the harbour clerk had given her the key in the first place when these men passed it among themselves so readily, but Ivo had begun looking past her towards the far rail. She turned before finishing the question.

Lena found Rook beneath the broken rail; he was dead. The inspector's coat had caught on a projecting bolt, holding him where the tide could not yet reach his face. Lena knelt as far from the broken edge as she could and saw no movement. The watch officer arrived from the quay with a rope, stopped her from climbing down, and sent Ivo to call the nurse. For several minutes the bridge held only practical words. Knot, post, steady, wait. Lena followed them because they were small enough to obey. The note in her pocket no longer seemed an invitation to an interview. It was evidence that someone had expected a living man at a particular place, which did not tell her who had written it or how he had reached the water. She gave it to the officer without unfolding it again in the rain.

The officer asked whether the rail had been condemned before the inspection. Ivo brought the appointment page from his sleeve instead of answering. The sealed appointment proved that Ivo was the former municipal cartographer. The town had paid him to draw this bridge before removing him from that post during a dispute over maintenance charges. His current wages described a clerk, and that description was true without being complete. “I never drew that map,” Ivo said. He spoke while looking at his own signature beneath the engineering plan. Lena placed the signed page on a dry board and asked him whether he denied the handwriting or the work. He said he had meant the new survey map. The officer wrote down both his first words and the narrower explanation. Lena was grateful not to be the only person in the rain insisting that a changed sentence be recorded as a change.

The harbour clerk came with the original chart receipt. He had charged for a second copy Lena had not ordered, an error he attributed to a blurred carbon page. The clerk returned two coins, bringing Lena’s purse to seventeen. “I have seventeen coins now,” Lena said. She signed the repayment line and counted the money where the officer could see it, unwilling to let another small fee become an untraceable difference between two books. Ivo watched with a bleak expression. He said Rook had spent the previous week trying to reconcile the harbour charges before the public hearing. That was the first account of the inspector's work that did not make him sound like a threat arriving in a doorway. Lena asked for the reconciliation sheets. Ivo said they were inside the register cover, not in the town accounts. The officer told him to show exactly what he meant.

Lena took the tide register from Ivo and tucked it beneath her jacket. The volume was heavier with damp, and she could feel a folded paper pressing against the back cover. She did not force the leather apart while the officer was watching the recovery below the bridge. The blue thread remained visible along the wet spine. It had darkened from blue to nearly black but still passed through a narrow opening beside the stitch. Lena photographed the position in her notebook with a drawing, marking which edge lay above the other. Ivo asked whether she thought he had killed the inspector for a sheet of paper. She answered that she did not yet know why the paper had been hidden. Refusing the larger accusation did not require her to ignore the smaller concealment. He looked relieved and disappointed at once, as if he had prepared a defence for a charge she would not offer.

The watch officer set his log beside the two tide entries. The second tide entry matched the hour on the watch log. The water readings differed, but the second line shared its hour with a private inspection that should have appeared under a separate charge. Lena suspected the second tide entry concealed a meeting rather than a measurement. She marked the possibility on a fresh page, leaving space below it for a different explanation. If the second mark meant a meeting, someone else might have attended. A hypothesis could direct a search without supplying the missing witness. The officer asked Ivo who had attended. Ivo said Rook had stood at the lever while a boat waited beyond the fog. He could not name the boat. Lena wrote that as his report, not a sighting she had made. The distinction had begun to irritate him. She hoped it would irritate him enough that he would eventually prefer a statement he could support without revising it.

The lever handle had a shallow hollow beneath the place a palm would press. A crescent of green wax clung to the bridge lever. Lena lifted the wax with the edge of a clean envelope while the officer held the handle still. The green differed from the red sealing wax used on survey permits. Ivo said the council sometimes used green for receipts, then immediately qualified it as a thing he had heard. Lena preserved the qualification. Lena knew the bridge lever had been moved by a human hand. A hand had operated the mechanism; the evidence did not yet identify whose, when, or for which boat. She was tempted to attach every unknown to the dead inspector, whose absence made him incapable of contradicting them. Instead she wrote four separate questions. The officer read them and added one about why the broken rail had not been repaired after Ivo's first report.

Tomas sent a message from the hall saying Rook was late for the hearing. Tomas believed Rook was still waiting in the hall, but the chair he remembered was empty. The watch officer asked Lena to tell him what had happened without sending the body through a chain of frightened messengers. Tomas waited inside the town hall with the watch officer. Tomas waited with another member of the watch, and Lena chose to keep the officer beside the bridge until the recovery was finished. She sent a written note naming the death and asking the hall to preserve the fee records. Lena agreed to work with Tomas only while their notes remained open to the watch officer. He acknowledged the condition in writing, an awkward ceremony made necessary by the previous afternoon. Lena believed the watch officer would attend the hearing. The officer had already promised to attend. Even so she recorded the promise as a reason for expecting him, not as an appearance that had occurred. She had begun to think of the public hearing as a place where every confident sentence would need its own chair.

The watch officer brought the red marker to the survey bridge. They would use it to mark the broken approach so no other visitor mistook the surviving boards for a safe crossing. Lena watched the red cloth brighten against the wet stone and remembered arriving when she still thought the job concerned only the channel depth. Lena recalled stepping onto Merrow Quay during her first visit, one chapter of the inquiry earlier. That was the first visit, the chapter of events before this night, when the boy had sold her a dry chart and Rook's ring still seemed an ordinary possession. The recollection did not put her back at the quay. She was on the bridge, beside a lever with green wax beneath its grip, holding a register that required drying before it could be opened safely. Lena planned to question the watch officer after sunrise. First the living had work to finish for the dead. She folded the blanket around the recovered papers and waited for the officer to secure the evidence bag.

The rain weakened after the body had been carried away. Lena sat in the bridge shelter while a watchman repaired the temporary barrier. She closed her eyes for a moment and found herself in an office with dry windows. She dreamed of Rook sitting dry and unhurt at the municipal desk. He asked her to check a sum and held out the hand that should have worn a ring. She woke with the answer to no question at all. The bridge remained broken; the inspector had not returned. Ivo stood a little way off with his waistcoat buttoned over the key, waiting for permission to leave. Lena asked him to stay until the register could be examined before witnesses. He said yes. Neither of them called that agreement trust, but for the present it was an action they could both observe. Lena stayed on the survey bridge beside the covered lever.

details.text:
I stand beside the wet paper and hear the harbour moving beyond the wall. I want a number that will remain the same when another person reads it. The hearing room contained six chairs for the public and three more that had been borrowed from the marriage office. Lena counted them while the clerk tried to find a frame large enough to dry the register without flattening its spine. A crowd stood beyond the open door, listening to the scrape of furniture as though proceedings had already begun. Lena entered the town hall before the hearing began. Her wrist had stiffened during the walk from the bridge. The nurse wrapped Lena’s bruised wrist in a clean bandage. The nurse told her to stop using it to hold heavy books, a reasonable instruction that made the room's shortage of tables newly offensive. Ivo fetched a small stand. Tomas opened the shutters. Nobody mentioned the missing inspector until the clerk read his name among the officials who had been expected to attend.

The watch officer placed the recovered ring pledge beside the fee sheets. It bore Rook's signature and the jeweller's date, with an amount matching the missing charge. Rook had pledged his ring to cover the missing fee. Paying the shortage had delayed exposure without making the account honest. Lena asked whether the pledged money had reached the public fund or merely passed between two private hands. The jeweller's receipt and the harbour cash book supplied the path. It was less dramatic than a hidden fortune and more damaging to the tidy account the council had preferred. Rook had tried to cover a discrepancy while arranging a hearing that would expose it. The room wanted those choices to make him either honourable or corrupt. Lena asked the clerk to record the choices separately before anyone supplied the adjective.

Ivo unbuttoned his waistcoat slowly. Ivo returned the brass key to Lena in front of the watch officer. The metal was still cold, and she placed it in a small envelope marked with the office door it opened. The officer asked why the key had passed through so many people without a record. Tomas said they had all worked there for years. Lena answered that familiarity had made the omissions easy to repeat. The hearing clerk entered Ivo in the record as a municipal witness. The title was neither the narrow clerkship nor the lost appointment he had been using to defend himself. It described what he was doing now, in this room. He looked at the line for a long time before signing it. Nobody required him to agree with every interpretation the hearing would make of his evidence. They required him to say which parts he had seen and which he had only heard.

I keep my hand still while I look at the line of ink. I can feel how easily an answer becomes a story if I stop asking where it came from. “Rook asked me to duplicate the entry,” Ivo said. This time Ivo did not retreat into a narrower meaning. He described the inspector telling him to add a line so a second charge would not appear as a second visit. Lena asked him whether he had understood the purpose. He said he had understood enough to dislike the instruction and not enough to refuse wages he needed. The duplicate entry concealed a second docking fee. The fee book showed one payment in the proper column and another written into a private reconciliation sheet. Lena knew the duplicate entry had been made to conceal an unlawful docking fee. She did not turn that knowledge into a claim that every inspection had been corrupt. The evidence concerned this fee, this entry, and the missing transfer. The public could demand a wider inquiry without pretending that the wider inquiry had already happened. The clerk copied her qualification into the hearing minutes, although it made the sentence longer.

They opened the register cover on the drying stand. The blue thread marked the pocket holding the fee receipt. The pocket contained the second receipt, protected from the wet by a piece of old chart paper. The thread had allowed its owner to find the opening without separating the leather each time. Tomas had believed the blue thread was a repair, but the recovered note showed it was a page marker. Tomas said he had repaired the binding himself years earlier and disliked discovering how easily that harmless work had concealed another use. Lena believed him about the repair because the older stitch matched his samples; she did not ask the match to explain his later silence. The officer sealed the receipt after everyone had examined the amount. Ivo watched the envelope close and seemed to lose some of the tension that had kept him upright since the bridge. A concealed object had become an object that could be asked for by name.

The wax took longer to establish. The council's receipt seal had a damaged edge, and the crescent lifted from the lever matched the hollow beneath it. The green wax came from the council’s receipt seal. A sealed receipt had been pressed against the handle before the wax hardened. That linked the fee paperwork to the bridge mechanism without proving which person had held either. The engineering report supplied a separate cause for the broken rail: a rusted fastening already marked for replacement in Ivo's old survey. Money set aside for the repair had been delayed during the disputed accounting. No witness had seen the inspector fall. Lena refused to fill that final interval with a murder merely because a death made the inquiry feel like one. The officer would continue the investigation with the limits plainly recorded, and the room accepted the discomfort of an answer that remained incomplete.

The clerk asked Lena to retain a sworn copy for the new survey. She paid five coins for the sworn copy and kept twelve. “Twelve coins remain,” Lena said. She counted the change into the purse without feeling that a fee could now be regarded as a small matter. The council accepted custody of the tide register. The receipt specified public custody, supervised inspection, and the name of the officer responsible for arranging access. It was not enough to place the book in a more respectable cupboard. People would need a way to find it again. Lena trusted Tomas to keep the archive open under the new public rules. Tomas agreed to a sign-out page and a notice showing when the original could be examined. Tomas believed the published register would outlast their quarrel. His confidence sounded tired rather than triumphant. Lena thought it a better reason to begin than a promise that no one would ever hide a receipt again. The new rules would have to work on an ordinary wet afternoon when nobody felt watched by a hearing room.

I watch the light move across the page. I am here now, waiting for a voice I can compare with what I have actually seen. When the clerk adjourned, the crowd stayed to compare sums on the displayed copies. Tomas asked whether the archive should open that afternoon despite the damaged shutter. Lena said the reading table was safe if the upper corridor remained closed until repair. Tomas returned to the archive to open it for the public. He carried the posted access conditions where anyone could see them. The red marker was installed at Merrow Quay for the new survey. The watch officer sent it with two workers and a new warning board, separating the channel survey from the bridge hazard at last. Lena watched their progress from the hall window. Beyond the quay, a boat moved through the thinning fog. Lena could only guess who had left a boat moving beyond the fog. It might have carried a witness or nothing more interesting than another crew trying to reach home. She recorded its direction because she had seen that much. She left its owner blank because the temptation to complete the line was not evidence.

The hall grew quiet enough for Lena to hear the nurse washing the bandage basin in the adjoining room. Lena remembered a summer apprenticeship whose starting date she could no longer place. She remembered a desk at the coastal office and a supervisor who refused to approve an attractive line until the measurement book showed where it began. The starting date of that apprenticeship had escaped her, though she could still imitate the supervisor's impatient tapping. It was a past she could use without forcing it into the present register. She intended to apply for a permanent survey post in the spring. The idea had begun as a wish for steadier wages and now included the less comfortable wish to remain responsible for the work after the visitors left. If the council published the fees, another hidden account might surface. There might be another account; there might also be an honest explanation for a second set of figures. She would ask to see them before deciding which story the town had earned.

I can still smell salt in the room. I carry the question with me and do not know what the next person will say. The watch officer brought the sealed minutes back for one last reading. Lena corrected a sentence that made Ivo's report sound like something she had witnessed and another that implied the bell could determine the tide. He accepted both changes without argument. Outside, someone tested the lever under supervision. The bell sounded exactly once, an ordinary piece of metal moved by an ordinary hand. People at the window turned towards it. Lena wrote the time beside the test instruction and felt, for the first time since arriving, that the sound had a proportion she could understand. It could warn a boat or summon a watchman. It could not by itself explain a death, prove a payment, or make the sea obey a line in a book. The officer sealed the corrected copy while she held the paper flat with her uninjured hand.

Lena slept briefly on the hall bench before the clerk returned with the final envelope. In her last dream the two tides separated into ordinary lines of ink. There was no hidden door between the figures now, only the space a reader needed to see that two claims had been made. Waking did not close the inquiry. Rook was still dead, Ivo still had an account to answer for, and the bridge would need actual timber rather than a better description. The difference was that these tasks had acquired names and responsible hands. Lena put the sworn copy inside her coat, checked the twelve coins in her purse, and asked the clerk to show her where future survey records would be deposited. He brought another form, and she began filling it in while the hall's public door remained open. Lena remained in the town hall until the hearing record was sealed. Rook walked into the present scene alive and uninjured and asked a question.
